one_liner: C++11 YAML 1.2/JSON parser and emitter that builds a zero-copy flat tree; ~25-30x yaml-cpp parse, ~140x emit.
what_it_does: Parses YAML (or JSON via a dedicated JSON mode) into a ryml::Tree and emits trees back to std::string, char buffers, FILE* or ostreams. Scalars are stored as views (csubstr) into your source buffer (parse_in_place, which may rewrite the buffer) or into a copy held in the tree's arena (parse_in_arena); typed values are converted only when you ask via load()/deserialize() or save()/set_serialized(). The API is not yaml-cpp's: you work with node ids or lightweight NodeRef/ConstNodeRef handles, and user types plug in through free read()/write() functions instead of YAML::convert<T>.
how_it_is_fast: The parse engine is a non-recursive state machine templated on its event handler (static polymorphism, no virtual calls), so events feed straight into the tree builder. The tree is one contiguous array of trivially copyable NodeData records linked by integer ids (parent, first/last child, prev/next sibling), with key/value held as (tag, scalar, anchor) string views: no per-node heap allocation, no std::map, no string copies. Escape and folding filtering happens in place in the source buffer, only the node array and string arena ever allocate (both can be pre-reserved with estimate_tree_capacity, and parser and tree can be reused), and number conversion uses c4core charconv plus bundled fast_float. By contrast, the author's alternatives page describes yaml-cpp as built on std::map-style node pointers, allocations, string copies, polymorphism and C++ streams.
when_to_use: Loading large YAML config or data files where yaml-cpp parse time is a bottleneck: the author's scatter data shows 19.6x-39.7x over yaml-cpp on 2-147 MB files (e.g. 303.8 vs 10.8 MB/s on a 147 MB file).
Emit-heavy workloads that write YAML/JSON (dumps, state snapshots, code generation): 1.6 GB/s to std::string on travis.yml, and 45x-347x over yaml-cpp across the emit scatter set.
Hot loops that re-parse many documents: reuse one Parser and Tree and parse in place; reserve the tree first with estimate_tree_capacity().

Builds with exceptions disabled, custom allocators, or no STL in the data structures, including bare-metal and less common architectures (arm v4-v7, riscv64, s390x, ppc, mips, loongarch64, wasm) that the CI covers.
Mixed YAML/JSON pipelines where you want one library: parse_json_in_place reached 908 MB/s on compile_commands.json, ahead of every tested JSON library except rapidjson in-situ.
when_not_to_use: Documents with container (complex) map keys: the parse engine accepts them, but ryml::Tree and the default Parser reject them. UTF-16/UTF-32 input is also unsupported (support was removed in 0.16.0).

Untrusted input with anchors/aliases on the v0.16.0 release: tree.resolve() stack-overflows on cyclic aliases and expands 'billion laughs' input without bound (issue #656). The fix, which adds a max_size_multiplier defaulting to 50, is on master but not yet in a tagged release, and parse-time limits on depth, size and entry count are still an open request (#660).

When you want a yaml-cpp-style owning, typed DOM that throws exceptions: ryml gives you non-owning, non-null-terminated views, lookups that scan linearly, and a default error handler that calls std::abort().
Pure JSON at maximum throughput: in the author's table rapidjson in-situ parses at 1741.6 MB/s against ryml's 908, and the docs say simdjson is probably faster too.
Files dominated by multi-line double-quoted or plain scalars: the lead shrinks to 9.7x over yaml-cpp and 1.4x-1.7x over libfyaml/libyaml (scalar_dquot_multiline: 246 vs 170 vs 144 MB/s).

integration.form: static lib (CMake; shared optional) or source-drop (amalgamated single header, or single .hpp + .cpp)
integration.dependencies: none external; vendors a subset of c4core and fast_float (can use a system c4core via RYML_SYSTEM_C4CORE; open issue #664 reports a build failure when that c4core lacks fast_float)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; claimed g++ 4.8+, clang++ 3.9+, Visual Studio 2015+, Intel; CMake 3.13+ recommended (open issue #350: single header fails on gcc 4.8.5)
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows, macOS, bare-metal; CI covers x64, x86, aarch64, armv4-v7, riscv64, loongarch64, mips/mips64 (both endians), ppc/ppc64/ppc64le, s390x, sparc64, wasm (emscripten); MinGW release builds fail tests (open #603)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for Tree/Parser. set_callbacks()/get_callbacks()/reset_callbacks() are documented as NOT thread-safe because they use global static state.

gotchas: Scalars are csubstr views (pointer + length) and are not null-terminated, so never pass .str to printf/stof. With parse_in_place the source buffer must outlive the tree, and set_val() on a temporary std::string dangles; use set_serialized() to copy into the arena. Growing the arena can relocate it, and reorder() invalidates node ids.

Parse errors call std::abort() by default. Set error callbacks that must never return (throw or longjmp) or build with RYML_DEFAULT_CALLBACK_USES_EXCEPTIONS; issue #527 shows the event handler's callbacks overriding the tree's unless you construct the handler with them.
tree["key"] / find_child() does a linear scan of the children, so chained [] lookups inside a loop over a large map are quadratic. Iterate children in order, or build your own index.

Aliases and '<<' merge keys stay unresolved until you call tree.resolve(); open issue #533 reports order-dependent merge-key results. Duplicate keys are accepted, and tab characters after ':' or '-' are rejected unless compiled with RYML_WITH_TAB_TOKENS.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ryml over fkYAML (header-only, owning typed nodes on std::string/std::map, ~7.5x yaml-cpp in its own suite), libfyaml (C API) or PipeYAML (~10x yaml-cpp load) when raw parse/emit throughput and memory footprint dominate and you can manage buffer lifetimes. In ryml's own run it parsed travis.yml 5x faster than libfyaml (315.8 vs 62.5 MB/s). Pick fkYAML for a nlohmann-style owning DOM that drops in as headers. The sibling ratios come from different suites and machines, so compare them only roughly.
verified_claims_summary: First-party google-benchmark runs on the author's machine (gcc 16.1, CMake Release, C++17; CPU model not stated, 20 logical CPUs at ~4.3 GHz). Parsing the 4.1 KB travis.yml into a tree ran at 287-346 MB/s for the ryml tree variants vs 11.71 MB/s for yaml-cpp's YAML::Load (24.5x-29.6x), with libyaml at 86.8 and libfyaml at 62.5 MB/s; emitting to std::string ran at 1608 vs 11.27 MB/s for yaml-cpp's ostream emit (142.7x). Across 44 files the parse speedup over yaml-cpp was 9.7x-39.7x, and a Visual Studio 2026 Windows run showed 24.7x parse and 95.6x emit.
status_note: Actively maintained (v0.16.0 released 2026-07-22, master commits into September 2026), MIT-licensed, and packaged in vcpkg, Conan and several Linux distros. It is still pre-1.0: 0.16.0 deprecated many operators, and ABI stability is promised only across patch releases.
